records.name: Honduras
records.summary:
Honduras is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the regional Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the region, outside the two largest countries.

sources.summary: Wikipedia 'Transfemicide' (fetched 2026-09-29): general concept article with substantial Honduras content — HRW's El Salvador/Guatemala/Honduras finding that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks (Guatemalan officials calling them 'not biological women'), and Vicky Hernandez v Honduras at the Inter-American Court as the leading transfemicide case. Background framing for the record's violence claims.

LAWG Education Fund report 'Left in the Dark': Honduras and El Salvador among the world's highest rates of violence against women/LGBTI persons; LGBTI persons — trans women especially — face major obstacles to justice; impunity driven by under-reporting, lack of police/prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional case mishandling (quote: institutions 'fail to effectively investigate and prosecute'). Explains why anti-trans violence goes unpunished.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers Central America's LGBT people being terrorised at home and fleeing for their lives.

HRW report (May 2009) 'Not Worth a Penny': Human Rights Abuses against Transgender People in Honduras - police rape, assault and extortion of trans people, the shape of transgender lives in Honduras, and relevant domestic laws.

GlobalGayz Honduras archive: dated index of LGBT news 2004-2011 with embedded excerpts — Aug 2004 church protest at state recognition of three gay groups; 2009-10 items ('Young LGBT Activist Murdered in Wave of Violence and Impunity', 'Extreme levels of violence against gay community', post-coup abuses); 2005 marriage/adoption-ban coverage. Source index corroborating the record's violence timeline rather than analysis.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Honduras: significant human-rights issues include violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption, and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.

Washington Blade (25 Sep 2017): trans activist and Asociacion Cozumel Trans co-founder (PINU party) ran for Congress in Francisco Morazan at the 26 Nov 2017 election — potentially the first openly trans officeholder; context: Kendra Stefani Jordany's 2017 primary win, Claudia Spellman's 2012 LIBRE run, Victoria Gomez seeking asylum in Spain after threats/attacks in Tegucigalpa. Evidence of both trans visibility and the security costs behind it.

records.name: El Salvador
records.summary:
El Salvador demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years, among the lowest anywhere; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception (an exceptional security regime) with mass arbitrary detention (tens of thousands imprisoned, over 75,000 reported, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

sources.summary: Foreign Policy (9 Mar 2020, Anna-Catherine Brigida): prosecution of the death of Camila Díaz Córdova, a transgender Salvadoran woman, as a hate crime — activists called it an advance toward El Salvador's first hate-crime homicide conviction while documenting continuing discrimination and abuse of LGBTQ citizens.

Dilemas journal article (Arévalo et al., Fundação Oswaldo Cruz, 2024): 'Denied deaths' builds a profile of crimes, victims and perpetrators of homicides against LGBTI+ people in El Salvador across 2000-2020 — the peer-reviewed longitudinal dataset on anti-LGBTI+ killings for the period.

HRW report 'Every Day I Live in Fear' (7 Oct 2020): El Salvador (with Guatemala and Honduras) fails to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, driving asylum claims to the US; documents obstacles to obtaining protection.

HRW report (Jan 2021) 'I'm Lucky to Still Be Alive': violence and discrimination against LGBT people in El Salvador - full report with recommendations to the president, attorney general, congress and ministries.

HRW (31 Jul 2020): San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of the January 2019 killing of transgender woman Camila Díaz Córdova and sentenced each to 20 years; the 28 July 2020 judgment is the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for killing a transgender person, hailed by HRW as pivotal for transgender Salvadorans' rights.

Washington Blade (9 Sep 2015): National Assembly approved legal-code reforms so killings motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender draw 30-60 years under Article 129 — the enhanced hate-crime penalty framework on the books since.

records.name: Costa Rica
records.summary:
Costa Rica is workable for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.

sources.summary: Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex conduct legal since 1971; first Central American country to adopt marriage equality (2020); since 2018 (Executive Decree 41173-MP) legal gender change on documents without surgery or court order; state health system funds gender-affirming care; rollback pressure — conversion-therapy bill stalled since its 2019 committee report, and in 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.
ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Costa Rica: documents LGBTI-related legal frameworks — status of same-sex conduct, gender recognition and protections.

UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, report on her July 2023 visit to Costa Rica (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024): praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific legislation; concerned about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups; recommends intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

GayLawNet Costa Rica legal reference: survivor's pension extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans (Ministry of Labor announcement 25 Jun 2016; individual survivor benefit approved 29 Jun 2018; teachers' separate budget excluded); also records the 2000 Supreme Court ruling that IVF is unconstitutional — dated partnership-benefits context.

PinkNews (1 May 2008): the Costa Rican government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia (17 May); President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directed public institutions to facilitate, promote and support activities 'directed at the eradication of homophobia' — credit to LGBT group CIPAC.

The Tico Times (16 May 2014): President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial on equal mast with the national flag for 17 May (officially recognised since 2008); lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other conservative parties called it a 'provocation' while a same-sex civil union bill was pending — organised political opposition alongside official recognition.

records.name: Panama
records.summary:
Panama is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery — a resident-facing barrier. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and in March 2023 the Supreme Court ruled same-sex marriage is not a constitutional right, signaling judicial conservatism. Panama City has a visible, established trans community and hosts regional LGBT organising.

No traveler-facing restrictions exist: no bathroom laws, no border friction, no documented police targeting pattern. Social hostility is moderate — machista culture persists, and trans women face documented employment exclusion — but violent targeting is far below Northern Triangle levels.

sources.summary: Outright International current Panama overview: amendment of the general anti-discrimination law to include SOGI grounds was blocked by the National Assembly in 2024 (claiming implicit coverage), no acts are formally recognised as hate crimes, intersex infant surgeries are not prohibited; at the 2025 UN UPR multiple states urged explicit anti-discrimination protections, gender-recognition reform and stronger violence safeguards — legal reforms remain stalled and Panama lags much of Latin America.

Equaldex data for Panama: homosexuality legal, marriage banned, gender change legal but requires surgery, no nonbinary recognition, no hate-crime protections, no employment/housing discrimination protections, blood donation banned (indefinite deferral), conversion therapy not banned. Only 12% approve of same-sex marriage (AmericasBarometer 2023, ranked #18 of 22).

Washington Blade (16 Feb 2018): Supreme Court Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega withdrew his October 2017 draft ruling against marriage rights — the draft had held the family code's same-sex marriage bars not unconstitutional while suggesting the Assembly consider civil unions; the Panama government signalled it would comply with the landmark 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision.

BBC features (14 Aug 2018): in Panama's Guna Yala indigenous territory a flourishing 'third gender' community (Omeggid) is accepted as completely normal, with powerful matriarchal figures elevating women's status — cultural context for how gender diversity is received in this part of the country.

Outright International current Panama overview (fetched page resolves to the country overview): anti-discrimination amendment blocked by the National Assembly in 2024, no hate-crime recognition, unregulated intersex infant surgery, 2025 UPR calls for SOGI protections and gender-recognition reform, reforms stalled.

Washington Blade (22 Oct 2017): La Estrella reported Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega's draft ruling finding the family-code sections barring same-sex marriage 'not unconstitutional' while leaving the National Assembly to legislate civil unions ('equality must be constitutionally guaranteed via the law'); the two marriage lawsuits (a UK-marriage recognition suit and a direct family-code challenge) were combined after summer 2017 oral arguments, with amicus briefs from regional marriage-equality advocates and public support from the First Lady, while Catholic and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition.

records.name: Dominican Republic
records.summary:
The Dominican Republic demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, and the 2024 Constitutional Court review of the remaining sodomy-law articles (210/260, which applied to police and armed-forces members) has resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations — though the existence of these articles revealed the institutional culture. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering SOGI (Brazil, a foreign government, formally recommended one at the 2024 UPR review), and documented violence against trans women is high, particularly affecting the most marginalised.

Tourist zones (Punta Cana, Puerto Plata) are heavily insulated resort enclaves with international norms; Santo Domingo, the capital, has a visible community and annual Pride caravan. Outside those bubbles, machista culture, police harassment of trans women (especially sex workers), and anti-Haitian (xenophobic) dynamics that compound for dark-skinned trans people are documented.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (30 Aug 2024): documented the Constitutional Court challenge to sodomy-law remnants reaching only police and military officers (no equivalent for heterosexual acts), with HRW's amicus brief arguing equality/privacy violations. SUPERSEDED per resolved review: The 2024 constitutional review of the sodomy-law remnants is resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations; still no anti-discrimination or marriage recognition.

UPR database (Sexual Rights Initiative): the Dominican Republic accepted recommendations on intersex persons' rights and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity — an accepted international-commitment record with no domestic implementation detail shown.

Time/Amnesty International (31 Mar 2019): TDOV conversation with two activists including Nairovi Castillo of the Dominican Republic, executive director of COTRAVETD (Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers, co-founded 2004) — first-hand account of trans struggles in the country.

Washington Blade (1 Apr 2017): 300+ activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT/intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo with Dominican government officials speaking — a marker of official-level engagement in 2017.

Washington Blade (27 Apr 2016): documents the backlash against openly gay US Ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster after his June 2015 presentation with his husband in Santo Domingo — framed as attacks on LGBT Dominicans, showing organised domestic opposition climate.

Washington Blade (3 Apr 2017): the openly gay US ambassador's departure left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence (spoke at Santo Domingo Pride, 3 Jul 2016) — trailing marker of the polarised climate his tenure exposed.

records.name: Canada
records.summary:
Canada is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code’s hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveller warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

sources.summary: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026): police-reported hate crime totalled 4,882 incidents in 2024 (+1% after a 34% jump in 2022-23); incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, down from a 2023 peak of 889 — three consecutive years of increases ended.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (timeout); the underlying page presents quick stats from the federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan survey findings.

Egale Canada UPR submission (2012): overview of LGBT human rights in Canada - sexual orientation in the Charter since 1995, marriage equality 2005; but trans protections limited and varying by jurisdiction, with no federal gender-identity discrimination law at the time; identifies gaps against the Yogyakarta Principles.

CBC News (Apr 2016): Prince Edward Island amended its Vital Statistics Act so a trans person changes the gender on official documents by declaring their identified gender plus a doctor's letter — the prior surgery requirement removed. A practical document-update pathway in one province.

The Globe and Mail (Jun 2017): the Senate passed Bill C-16 by 67-11, prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression and adding gender identity/expression to the Criminal Code hate-motivation provisions — framed as Canadian leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash.

Ontario Human Rights Commission policy (Part I): lays out the legal context, case law and legislation for sexual-orientation discrimination complaints under the Ontario Human Rights Code, which expressly covers gender identity and gender expression — official Ontario guidance a visitor/resident can invoke for discrimination recourse.
